summary: Marcus, the narrator of this excerpt from Book 1 (part 52), describes his new life after the Department of Homeland Security-style surveillance crackdown in San Francisco. He has abandoned his old handle, set up an anonymous email through the Swedish Pirate Party, and relies on the Xnet network, while helping others with Xnet troubleshooting. He mourns the suspension of the Harajuku Fun Madness game, deliberately tapers his use of his wiretapped laptop, and distributes fifty to sixty burned copies of ParanoidXbox daily. He defends his confidence in encryption by explaining the basic idea of one-way mathematical functions, using multiplying large primes as the example.
one_line: The narrator, now using the handle M1k3y, evades surveillance via the Xnet and the Pirate Party email while distributing ParanoidXbox and explaining cryptography basics.
key_facts: The narrator set up a fake email address through the Pirate Party, a Swedish political party that hated Internet surveillance.
The narrator accessed his email strictly via Xnet, hopping from one neighbor's Internet connection to the next.
The narrator's new handle, come up with on the spur of the moment, was M1k3y, replacing w1n5ton.
The narrator said that if Benson could figure out w1n5ton, anyone could.
The company suspended Harajuku Fun Madness indefinitely, citing "security reasons" about hiding things and sending people to find them.
The narrator kept using his laptop but planned to use it a little less each day so watchers would see a gradual change in habits.
The narrator read obituaries of thousands of friends and neighbors dead at the bottom of the Bay.
The narrator burned fifty or sixty copies of ParanoidXbox every day and handed them out around the city.
The narrator said Crypto is cryptography, or "secret writing", and has existed since Roman times.
The narrator said Augustus Caesar was a big fan of secret codes and liked to invent his own.
The narrator described crypto as hard math and gave the Cliff's Notes version: some mathematical functions are easy in one direction and hard in the other.
The narrator gave the example that multiplying two big prime numbers together to make a giant number is easy, while reversing it is hard.
